entries.name: The Hutterite Brethren
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Rich in inside voice. The Brethren's own chronicle runs to 1665. It is printed in Wolkan's edition of 1923. Beck's edition of 1883 adds their later records and the state's orders against them, up to 1785. Both are in German, and no public-domain English version exists.
entries.relationsSummary: The Hutterites grew out of the Anabaptist church at Nikolsburg in 1528. Habsburg rulers hunted them. They burned Jakob Hutter in 1536. In 1622 they drove the Brethren out of Moravia. From 1757 the government in Hungary broke up the last of their homes. A few families kept the faith and moved on to Russia.
entries.why: In 1528 a band of Anabaptists left Nikolsburg in Moravia. On the road their leaders spread a cloak on the ground. Everyone laid down their goods on it, freely and unforced. From that act came a church that held all its goods in common. It took its name from Jakob Hutter, burned in 1536. Its own chronicle tells the story from the inside.
entries.longDescription:
In 1528 Jakob Widman led his followers out of Nikolsburg in Moravia. They were some two hundred people, not counting the children. They had parted from the Anabaptists there who kept the sword. In a deserted village on the road, their leaders spread a cloak on the ground. Everyone laid down their goods on it, freely and unforced. They pointed to the prophets and the apostles.

Jakob Hutter led the community for more than two years. In 1535 he was betrayed and seized at Klausen, and taken to King Ferdinand's government at Innsbruck. He was tortured and then burned alive early in 1536. The Brethren took his name, and their chronicle says they were not ashamed of it.

The communities spread across Moravia. By 1622, the Brethren said, they had lived there more than eighty years and served many lords well. That October the emperor Ferdinand drove them out of all Moravia. They left twenty-four households behind, with their grain, wine and herds. They went into Hungary with almost nothing, as winter set in.

In Hungary and Transylvania they lived on for some decades more, growing fewer. From 1757 the government broke up the last communities, and most members became Catholics. A few families would not give up their fathers' faith. They moved to Wischenka in Russia, and in 1784 others fled to join them.
entries.teaser: Moravia, Hungary and Transylvania, 1528 to 1785 — Anabaptists who laid their goods on one cloak. They held all things in common, and their chronicle tells what it cost them.
voices: Jakob Hutter — leader of the community, seized at Klausen in 1535 and burned in 1536, whose letters survive and whose name the Brethren took
Peter Riedemann — a minister of the community, jailed at Nuremberg from 1533, author of its account of its faith, the Rechenschaft
entries.legacy: The Brethren never let their chronicle go. Beck found their families in Russia, near the Sea of Azov, by 1852. In 1874 the Brethren moved from Russia to America and took the book with them. In 1923 the Hutterian Brethren in Canada published it, as a house book for every member.

livingEvidence.basis: A living tradition whose own chronicle travels with it. Beck (1883) traces the families from Hungary to Russia, and to a colony near the Sea of Azov from 1852. Wolkan's preface (1923) says the Brethren who left Russia for America in 1874 still held the chronicle, and their colony in Alberta published it. Nothing later is in the Library.

entries.name: The Mennonites and the Amish
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward part of an earlier entry; not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Thin for this period. The shelf holds later printings of older texts. The Martyrs Mirror of 1660 is here in an English edition of 1886. The Ausbund hymnal is here in Pennsylvania printings of 1846 and 1856. The Dordrecht Confession of 1632 is here in an Indiana manual of 1890. Their prefaces speak for the later church. From the 1700s, only the Ephrata chronicle tells of them, and it speaks from outside.
entries.floorNote: No question. Their Dordrecht Confession says that the Word became "flesh and man", born of the Virgin Mary.
entries.relationsSummary: These churches were heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists. The Mennonites of Pennsylvania asked the Ephrata Brethren to print their book of martyrs in German. A church manual of 1890 tells of Amish churches too.
entries.why: After 1650 the heirs of the Anabaptists became settled churches. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht gathered their martyrs into one great book, the Martyrs Mirror. He longed to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters". The book crossed the sea with his people. In Pennsylvania the Ephrata Brethren printed it in German, and in 1886 an English edition came out.
entries.longDescription:
After 1650 the heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists lived on as settled churches. Many were called Mennonites, after Menno Simons. Their Dordrecht Confession of 1632 stayed their rule of faith. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht published the Martyrs Mirror. It told of those "Who Baptized Only Upon Confession of Faith". In a prayer dated at Dort in 1659, he asked to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters".

In Pennsylvania the Mennonites wanted their great martyr book in German, not Dutch. The Ephrata community in Lancaster County did the work. Fifteen of its brothers were set to it, and the job took three years. The edition ran to 1300 copies.

The old hymn book of the Swiss Brethren, the Ausbund, was printed again and again in Pennsylvania. Its songs, the title says, were written in the prison at Passau. A Lancaster printing of 1856 calls itself the seventh in Pennsylvania. In 1886 Mennonite publishers brought out the Martyrs Mirror in English. English was spreading "year by year" among "our Mennonite people", its preface says.

In 1890 a manual from Elkhart set out the church's forms. A minister was chosen by lot. A slip with a verse from Proverbs went into one of several like books. The man whose book held it was ordained. Some congregations, "especially among the Amish and Russian Mennonites", chose by the members' vote instead.
entries.teaser: The Netherlands, Pennsylvania and Indiana, 1650 to 1890 — heirs of the Anabaptists. They carried a book of their martyrs across the sea and kept printing it.
voices: Thieleman J. van Braght — compiler of the Martyrs Mirror (1660), whose prefaces and prayer are dated at Dort in 1659
The publishers of the English edition of 1886 — Mennonites who called the martyrs "especially precious to us"
entries.legacy: The martyr book still speaks for these churches. In 1886 its publishers called the martyrs "especially precious to us, as Mennonites". Through them, they wrote, God handed down what "we hold and practice at the present day". The churches live on, but the Library does not yet hold their story after 1890.

livingEvidence.basis: The church's own prefaces claim the martyrs as its forebears, from van Braght (1659) to the English edition of 1886. The grade Documented covers the Mennonite line. The Amish descent is shown only by one mention, in the Elkhart manual of 1890, pending the source pass. The Amish division of the 1690s is not yet in the Library, and no inside text after 1890 is.

entries.name: The Melkite Greek Catholic Church after 1815
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing: Moderate, and mostly the record of its offices and councils. The church's synods from 1816 to 1902 survive in Latin and Italian, printed in 1911. A French history of 1910 and 1911 covers the rule of Maximos Mazloum and the church's later life. No Arabic sermon, letter or chronicle of the period is yet in the Library.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the church of the 1724 split at Antioch, carried on by the same line of patriarchs. It stayed in communion with Rome. In 1831 Rome's mission office called its bishops together in synod. In 1848 a decree of the sultan gave it a civil standing of its own.
entries.why: In the nineteenth century the Melkite Catholics won a place of their own. Their bishops met again and again in synod to choose patriarchs. Maximos III Mazloum, patriarch from 1833 to 1855, won a decree from the sultan in 1848. From then on, Cyril Charon wrote in 1910, the Melkite Catholics were fully free in civil matters.
entries.longDescription:
Patriarch Macarius Tauil died on 15 December 1815. Only four bishops were left. In June 1816 they met at the monastery of Saint Anthony on Mount Lebanon. There they chose the priest Moses Qattan as patriarch.

Under Qattan the church's affairs went from bad to worse. So Rome's mission office, the Propaganda, told its delegate to gather all the bishops. They met late in 1831 at the Annunciation monastery at Zuq Mikhail.

Maximos III Mazloum was elected patriarch in 1833. He wrote to the pope at once to ask for confirmation. In 1835 he held a national council at Ain Traz. From 1843 to 1848 he worked in Constantinople. There he won the sultan's decree of 7 January 1848. It gave the Melkite Catholics full civil standing of their own.

In 1849 Maximos presided over a council of his church at Jerusalem. He died at Alexandria in August 1855, and the bishops chose Clement Bahus. In 1858 Clement asked all his people to keep the Gregorian calendar. Four of his bishops rose against him. In 1859 they met at Zahle and declared him stripped of all authority.

The synods went on choosing patriarchs. Peter Geraigiri was elected at the monastery of Sarba in 1898. After his death, Cyril VIII Geha was elected on 27 June 1902. Rome confirmed him a year later, and he still led the church in 1911.
entries.teaser: Damascus and Mount Lebanon, 1815 to 1911 — the Melkite Catholic patriarchs and their synods. In this century the church won a civil standing of its own.
voices: Maximos III Mazloum — patriarch from 1833 to 1855, who won the sultan's decree of 1848
Agapios Riachi — metropolitan of Beirut, one of four bishops whose 1859 letter from Zahle against their patriarch survives in the French they sent to Rome
entries.legacy: The civil standing won in 1848 lasted. Writing in 1910, Charon says it still held in his day. Through these years the bishops chose each patriarch in synod, and Rome then confirmed him. The church lives on, but the Library does not yet hold its story after 1911.

livingEvidence.basis: The same see and the same line of patriarchs. The synod of 1816 chose a successor to Macarius Tauil. Charon (1910-1911) names Cyril VIII Geha, elected in 1902, as the patriarch of his own day. Nothing after 1911 is in the Library.

set.longDescription: In January 1525 a handful of men in Zurich baptized one another as adults. They were impatient with how slowly their own city's reform was moving, and they were hunted for it. Anabaptists held that baptism belonged to those who could confess faith for themselves. The church, they said, was a free body of believers, not a whole society. Most of them also held that a Christian could neither swear oaths nor take up the sword. Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed rulers alike saw them as a threat to order. By one early count more than two thousand were put to death, above all in Catholic lands. The survivors regrouped. In Moravia, a band that pooled its goods in 1528 grew into the Hutterite Brethren. In the Low Countries, a former priest named Menno Simons gathered congregations, and their descendants still carry his name.

neighbor_changes.reason: The Hutterites now have their own entry, which tells their communal life. The Anabaptist text keeps one sentence naming where they came from, so the two do not tell the same story twice. continuesAs: the Swiss and Dutch wings carry on as the new Mennonite and Amish entry (era 7 to 8, adjacent); the Hutterites leave by a 'gave rise to' link instead.

It was null only because no Melkite entry after 1815 existed (the Armenian change order of 2026-11-08 cites it as the pattern for an Eastern Catholic strand with no successor). The 1816 synod at Saint Anthony elected the successor of Macarius Tauil (d. 15 December 1815), so the same see and church continue (era 8 to 9, adjacent).
